s443: The welcome team at a church in Ludhiana, Punjab, led by Harpreet, 41
s444: Harpreet led the church welcome team, but meetings often ended in tension. Jaspreet, a loud and cheerful extrovert, wanted to greet everyone at the door and plan big events. Thomas, a quiet and careful introvert, preferred working behind the scenes, tracking new visitors and sending follow-up messages. Ruth, an older member, loved praying with people one by one. Each person thought their way was the right way. Jaspreet called Thomas unfriendly. Thomas thought Jaspreet was shallow. Ruth felt ignored. New visitors noticed the tension and rarely came back. One Sunday, a visiting family left after the service without anyone speaking to them, because each team member assumed someone else would do it. Harpreet went home discouraged and prayed, Lord, why can we not work together?
s445: Research suggests teams with a mix of personalities can be very effective, but only when members value each other's styles. When differences are not understood, people tend to judge others by their own preferences. This is a natural bias, as our brains often see our way as normal and other ways as wrong. Under pressure, the alarm system makes people more defensive and less curious. Jaspreet's energy, Thomas's careful follow-up and Ruth's prayerful presence were each strengths, but they were competing rather than combining. Each had grown up in a home or church where only one type of service was praised. Understanding personality as a range of gifts helps teams move from rivalry to partnership.
s446: Harpreet led a session where each member named their strengths and what drained them. They realised that they were not rivals but pieces of one plan. They redesigned the welcome so every person could serve in their strongest way.
s447: Each member shares their strengths and drains
s448: Assign greeting, follow-up and prayer roles clearly
s449: Create a simple handover from door to follow-up
s450: Thank one teammate for their strength each month
s452: Paul describes the church as one body with many members. For as the body is one, and hath many members ... so also is Christ (1 Corinthians 12:12). He goes on, If the whole body were an eye, where were the hearing? (1 Corinthians 12:17). Romans 12:6 says, Having then gifts differing according to the grace that is given to us, let us use them. Peter writes, As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another (1 Peter 4:10). Ephesians 4:16 speaks of the whole body fitly joined together. Differences are not a problem in God's family. They are the plan.
s453: God loves variety. He did not create a church of identical people but a body of many parts. Extroverts often bring warmth and energy, introverts bring depth and care, and others bring prayer, wisdom or practical help. Each one reflects a different side of God's character. When people use their strengths together, the result is far richer than any single style could produce. God designed us to need one another, which keeps us humble and reminds us that no one person can do everything.
s454: 1 Peter 4:10|As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another
s458: The team still had disagreements. Jaspreet sometimes forgot to pass names to Thomas, and Thomas occasionally felt overwhelmed during busy festival services. But visitors began to return. One family said they felt welcomed at the door, followed up kindly and prayed for personally. Team meetings grew lighter and more honest. Members started to appreciate rather than criticise one another.
s459: A team flourishes when each person's strength is valued and woven together.
s460: In a team, some people are loud and some are quiet. When everyone uses their own gift, the team works better.
s461: The Man Whose Temper Softened Over Years
s462: Rajesh, 52, a businessman in Jaipur, Rajasthan
s463: Rajesh had always been known for his temper. His employees feared his shouting, and his children stayed in their rooms when he came home. He told himself it was simply his nature. My father was like this and so am I, he would say. When he gave his life to Christ at 45 through a friend's invitation to church, he hoped the anger would vanish overnight. It did not. He still exploded at traffic, at his staff and at his wife. Each time, he felt ashamed and wondered whether his faith was real. One evening his teenage son said, Papa, you pray at church but you shout at home. Rajesh felt the words cut deep. He knelt in his office that night and asked God to change him, however long it took.
s464: Research suggests some people are born with a more intense temperament, reacting quickly and strongly to frustration. Rajesh had also grown up watching his father shout, so anger became his default way to handle stress. His alarm system fired fast, and his thinking brain had little practice in calming it. Each outburst strengthened that pathway. Personality is partly inherited, but research also shows that people tend to become calmer and more agreeable with age, and deliberate practice can add to this change. Character is shaped by daily choices, role models, community and, for Christians, the work of the Holy Spirit. Rajesh's temperament would not disappear, but its expression could be transformed.
s465: A pastor told Rajesh that the fruit of the Spirit grows slowly, like a mango tree. He did not need to become a different person overnight. He needed to keep walking with God and practising new responses day by day.
s466: Notice early body signs of anger rising
s467: Take a short pause and breathe before speaking
s468: Apologise quickly to anyone he hurts
s469: Meet weekly with a mentor for accountability
s470: Review each day with God using the fruit of the Spirit
s471: Scripture promises real change, but it often comes through patient growth. Galatians 5:22-23 says, the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance. Fruit takes time to ripen. James 1:19-20 tells us to be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath: For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God. Philippians 1:6 says, he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ. Peter, once quick to anger and impulsive, became a steady shepherd of the church. God works through our efforts, as Philippians 2:12-13 shows, for it is God which worketh in you.
s472: God designed both our temperament and our ability to grow. A strong, intense temperament can carry courage, passion and drive, which are good gifts when shaped by love. God also made the brain able to form new pathways through repeated practice. When the Holy Spirit works in us and we take small steps of obedience, our reactions slowly change. This design shows God's patience. He does not discard us for our weaknesses. He works with what He made, refining it like a potter shaping clay over time.
s473: Galatians 5:22-23|But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance
s477: Change was slow and uneven. In the first year, Rajesh still had many outbursts and sometimes felt like giving up. But he kept apologising and meeting his mentor. Over five years, his staff noticed he spoke more calmly. His son began to come out of his room when Rajesh came home. He still has a quick temper on hard days, but now he catches it sooner and repairs faster.
s478: God transforms even a harsh temperament through the Spirit and patient practice over years.
s479: Some people get angry easily. With God's help and practice, they can slowly learn to be calm and gentle.
s480: The Student Who Found Her Strengths
s481: Sneha, 19, a first-year college student in Guwahati, Assam
s482: Sneha was painfully shy in her first year of college. She sat at the back of every class and ate lunch alone. The other students seemed confident, funny and full of ideas. Sneha felt invisible and wondered whether she had anything to offer. She joined the college Christian fellowship but stayed silent in meetings, thinking her thoughts were not important. At home in her village she had been known as the helpful one who cared for younger cousins, but in the big college she felt like no one. One evening, after a lonely day, she cried in her hostel room and asked God why He had made her so quiet. She wished she could be bold like the others and believed her quiet nature was a mistake.
s483: Research suggests shyness is common, especially in new and unfamiliar settings, and often eases as people gain experience and confidence. Sneha's temperament was naturally reserved, and moving from a small village to a large city overwhelmed her nervous system. She compared herself to outgoing students and overlooked her own strengths. Research on character strengths shows that qualities like kindness, perseverance, love of learning and fairness are just as valuable as boldness. Many people do not notice their strengths because they seem ordinary to them. Sneha's family had valued her helpfulness but had rarely named it as a gift. Discovering and using strengths can build confidence and a sense of belonging.
s484: A senior in the fellowship asked Sneha to help organise a prayer list. As Sneha quietly followed up with each person, they felt cared for. The senior told her, You have a gift of kindness and faithfulness. Sneha began to see that her quiet ways were strengths.
s485: List three strengths others have noticed
s486: Use one strength in a new way each week
s487: Join a small group rather than a large crowd
s488: Speak one sentence in each fellowship meeting
s489: Thank God for how He made her
s490: God often chooses quiet people for important work. Psalm 139:14 says, I am fearfully and wonderfully made. 1 Peter 3:4 praises the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price. Dorcas was known not for speeches but for being full of good works and almsdeeds (Acts 9:36). Paul writes, For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works (Ephesians 2:10). Romans 12:6 reminds us we have gifts differing according to the grace given to us. Every member of God's family has something precious to offer, even when it is quiet.
s491: God made people with a wide range of strengths, and many of them are quiet. Kindness, faithfulness, careful listening and love of learning often work behind the scenes but hold communities together. God designed us so that we discover our gifts through serving and through others noticing them. Shyness may soften with time, but even if it remains, it does not cancel the strengths God has placed in us. His design ensures that every person has a place, and that the body of Christ needs both quiet and bold members.
s492: Ephesians 2:10|For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works
s496: Sneha still felt shy, especially in large groups. In her second semester she missed several fellowship meetings when assignments piled up, and she felt the old loneliness return. But she kept serving through the prayer list. By her second year, she led a small group of new students. She found two close friends and a sense of belonging she had not expected.
s497: Quiet strengths are real gifts, and discovering them helps us find our place.
s498: Some people are quiet, but they still have special gifts from God, like being kind or helpful. Using those gifts helps them belong.
